newsitem.title: USA: Dont' recruit ex-Soviet states, Russia tells NATO.
newsitem.headline: Dont' recruit ex-Soviet states, Russia tells NATO.

text.p: Russia will review relations with NATO if the Western defence alliance offers membership to former Soviet republics, Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Saturday.

"If NATO really expands at the expense of former Soviet republics, it will force us to look again at the whole system of relations with NATO," he told a news conference at the summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations.
Primakov was merely reiterating the tough line Russian officials have taken in recent weeks to try to deter NATO from any efforts to lure in former outposts of the Soviet Union.
But his remarks were a sober reminder of the differences that remain between Russia and the West, despite the mutual backslapping that has dominated the G7 summit.
Russia signed a partnership deal with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation in May which put relations between the former Cold War foes on a new footing.

The deal eased some of Moscow's concerns over NATO's plans to offer membership to at least three former communist states in eastern Europe in July, and Russia won the consolation prize of a bigger role than it has previously had at G7 conclaves.
But Russia and the West appear in recent weeks to have been marking out battle lines in readiness for what could be a confrontation over any second wave of NATO expansion.

Moscow has said repeatedly that it would not accept other former Soviet republics joining NATO because it is a security threat. It would also threaten Russia's drive towards greater economic integration with its ex-Soviet partners.
Russian officials have done their utmost to avoid discussion of NATO's expansion plans at the summit.

Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky has repeatedly told reporters it has not been a major focus of any talks involving Yeltsin, including when he met U.S. Presient Bill Clinton before the summit started on Friday.
Russia is particularly concerned that NATO might offer membership to the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia and to its fellow Slav neighbour Ukraine.
Lithuanian membership of NATO would mean Russia was completely cut off by NATO members from its small enclave of Kaliningrad, bordering Lithuania and Poland.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are expected to be offered membership at a NATO summit in Madrid next month.
The West has not ruled out that former Soviet republics could eventually join NATO and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright has sent encouraging signals to Latvia.
"Our goal is an integrated Europe. That goal embraces Latvia," she said last week.
Although Russia won a say in some security matters under its new partnership deal with NATO, it cannot veto the group's expansion.
